Court of Appeal Case No: CA/ HCC/0250/2025

2 | P a g e
Before : P. Kumararatnam, J.
Pradeep Hettiarachchi, J.
Counsel : Hejaaz Hisbullah with Chalana Perera and Uvindu
Kuruwitabandara for the Accused-Appellant
: Akila Dalpatadu SC for the Complainant-Respondent
Argued on : 16.07.2026
Decided on : 02.10.2026
Pradeep Hettiarachchi, J
Judgment
1. The Accused-Appellant (hereinafter referred to as “the Appellant”) was indicted
before the High Court of Negombo on the count of the murder of one Ranaweera
Arachchige Shriyani Ranaweera, an offence punishable under Section 296 of the
Penal Code.
2. Upon the election made by the Appellant for a trial without a jury, the trial against
him commenced and proceeded before the learned Judge of the High Court of
Negombo. During the trial, the prosecution led evidence of several lay witnesses as
well as of official witnesses, including that of the Judicial Medical Officer.
3. When the Trial Court called for the defence, the Appellant made a statement from
the dock and called a witness to testify on his behalf.
4. In delivering her judgment, the learned High Court Judge convicted the Appellant
for a lesser offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section
3 | P a g e
297, as the evidence showed that the offence was committed on the basis of a sudden
fight between the Appellant and the deceased.
5. Consequently, the Appellant was accordingly sentenced to 15 years’ rigorous
imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 10,000/-, carrying a default sentence of 6 months’
simple imprisonment. Further, the learned High Court Judge ordered the Appellant
to pay compensation to the aggrieved party of Rs. 500,000/-, in default of which,
one years’ simple imprisonment.
6. It is against the said conviction and sentence that the Appellant has preferred the
present appeal.
7. The prosecution’s case was entirely based on circumstantial evidence. The principal
contention advanced by the Appellant is that the circumstantial evidence adduced
at the trial does not give rise to the only irresistible inference of the Appellant’s guilt
and, therefore, falls short of the standard required to sustain a conviction.
8. Since the prosecution case is founded entirely on circumstantial evidence, it is
necessary to highlight the relevant items of evidence that were presented by the
prosecution before the Trial Court.
9. The alleged incident occurred on 27.11.2012 at the residence of the deceased, where
she was subsequently found dead inside her room. PW1, the elder daughter of the
deceased, testified on behalf of the prosecution. According to her evidence, the
deceased had been in a relationship with the Appellant for approximately one and
half years. However, PW1 testified that she did not know whether the deceased had
married the Appellant. She further testified that the Appellant frequently visited the
residence. However, approximately two weeks prior to the deceased’s death, the
Appellant and the deceased had an argument, following which the Appellant did not
visit the house until the day of the alleged incident.
4 | P a g e
10. On the day in question, the Appellant arrived at the residence at about 7.00 pm. At
the time of his arrival, PW1, her daughter, the deceased, and the mother of the
deceased were present in the house. PW1 opened the door for the Appellant and
informed the deceased of his arrival. The deceased thereafter came and
accompanied the Appellant to the first room of the house, where they ordinarily
resided. PW1 testified that the Appellant was wearing a shirt and a pair of trousers,
although she was unable to recall the colour or any particular features of the
clothing. She further testified that, while entering the house, the Appellant kept one
of his hands behind his body throughout the period during which she observed him.
However, PW1 testified that she did not see what, if anything, the Appellant was
concealing.
11. PW1 further testified that, at about 7.30 pm., when she went to bed with her
daughter, she heard an argument between the Appellant and the deceased. She
testified that following the Appellant’s arrival, she did not open the door for any
other person and that, before retiring to bed, she had closed all the doors and
windows of the house. However, PW2 did not testify as to whether she had locked
the doors of the house so as to prevent any person from entering the premises.
“ප්‍ර: තමුන් නිදා ගන්න යනක ාට නිවක ේ කදාර ජකනල් වහලද ගිකේ?
උ: ඔව්.” (at vide page 57 of the Appeal Brief)
12. The following morning, she discovered that her mother had been killed inside her
room. She accordingly called 119, following which the police arrived at the scene.
PW1 testified that, by the following morning, the main door of the house was found
to be open.
13. During the cross-examination, PW1 testified that she was employed as a receptionist
at the Cinnamon Grand Hotel. She testified that her shifts were ordinarily from 1.00
p.m. to 10.00 p.m. and from 6.00 a.m. to 4.00 p.m. It was further elicited in cross-
examination that there was a window in the house which was not kept locked and
through which a person could easily enter the premises. PW1 testified that on some
5 | P a g e
occasions, she herself used that window to enter the house after completing a night
shift. On the day of the incident, the said window was left open.
“ප්‍ර: ඔය අම්මා රක්ෂිත බන්ධනාගාර ගතව ඉන්න අව ේථා වලදී ඔබතුමිය කගදර එන
ක ාට කගදර අයට රදරයක්ෂ නි ා ඇතුල් කවන තැන වම් පැත්කත් ජකන්කල්
ඇතුකලන් අගුල දන්කන් නැතුව තිබුන කන්ද?
උ: ජනකල් නිතරම ඇරලා තිබුකන්.
ප්‍ර: එ එළිකයන් වහලා තිබුනට ඇතුකලන් අගුල දාලා තිබුකන් නැහැ?
උ: ඇතුකලන් අගුලක්ෂ දාලා තිබුකන් නැහැ.
ප්‍ර: නිතරම ඇරලා තිබුන කියන එ තමයි ඔබ කියන්කන්?
උ: එකහමයි.” (at vide page 72 of the Appeal Brief)
14. It was further elicited that the deceased had previously been named as a suspect in
several drug-related cases and had allegedly been obtaining money from persons by
way of extortion. Further, the deceased had been remanded in connection with those
cases.
15. The next witness called by the prosecution was PW4, who was serving in the Civil
Security Department. According to his testimony, on the night of the alleged
incident, at approximately 11.00 p.m. to 12.00 midnight, he observed a person
whom he believed to be similar in appearance to the Appellant, at a location
approximately 2 to 21/2 kilometers from the residence of the deceased. At the
relevant time, PW4 was traveling in a three-wheeler. He testified that he observed
the said person standing near a canal and attempting to stop a vehicle. According to
PW4, the person was wearing a black coloured T-shirt and a pair of trousers.
16. PW4 further testified that he identified the person as the Appellant by the light
emitted from the street lamps situated near the canal. He testified that he was able
to identify the Appellant by his beard. However, during cross-examination, PW4
admitted that he had assumed or inferred that the person was the Appellant on
account of the beard. It was further elicited that persons of the Muslim community
predominantly inhabited the relevant area.
6 | P a g e
“ප්‍ර: එතක ාට තමා ඔබ කිව්කව් කම් වකේ ක කනක්ෂ දැක්ෂ කියලා?
උ: ඔව්.
ප්‍ර: ඒ වකේම එම ප්‍රකේශය ඉ ේලාම් භක්ෂති යන් විශාල ප්‍රමාණයක්ෂ වා ය රන
ප්‍රකේශයක්ෂ?
උ: ඔව්.
ප්‍ර: රැවුල වවල තිබුණු පුේගලකයක්ෂ නි ා ඔබ කග ේ් ල ඔබ හිතුව කම් වකේ
පුේගලකයක්ෂ කවන්න ඇති කියලා ඔබ හිතුකව් එකහමයි?
උ: ඔව්.” (at vide page 95 of the Appeal Brief)
17. In the circumstances, the evidence of PW4 does not amount to a positive or reliable
identification of the Appellant. Significantly, PW4 himself admitted that he merely
assumed that the person he observed was the Appellant because of his beard.
Accordingly, his evidence cannot safely be relied upon as establishing that the
person observed by him was in fact the Appellant.
18. PW6, the Assistant Superintendent of Police, was also called as a witness for the
prosecution. According to his testimony, the police received the first information
regarding the alleged incident through a 119 call on 27.11.2012 at about 7.50 a.m.
He further testified that the police officers arrived at the scene of the alleged offence
at about 8.00 a.m. on the same day.
19. PW6 testified that, on 07.12.2012 at about 5.00 hours, he arrested the Appellant at
Kadawatha. He further testified that, on 08.12.2012 at about 6.30 hours, pursuant to
a statement made by the Appellant, he recovered a black-coloured shirt, a pair of
trousers and a knife under and in terms of Section 27(1) of the Evidence Ordinance.
According to PW6, the said items of clothing were recovered from the residence of
the Appellant’s mother, while the knife was recovered from a canal situated near
the residence of the deceased. The knife was allegedly concealed beneath Japan
Jabara. PW6 testified that at the time of its recovery, there appeared to be blood on
the knife, which was produced under PR No. 195/12.
“ප්‍ර: මහත්මය ඒ අනුව කම් පිහිය ක ායා ගැනීමක්ෂ සිදු රන්කන් ක ායි ේථානකයන්ද?
7 | P a g e
උ: මුතුරාජකවල මරණ රියකේ නිවා ඉදිරිපිට ඇල මාර්ගකේ තිබිල.” (at vide page
154 of the Appeal Brief)
20. However, during cross-examination, PW6 admitted that he had produced two
affidavits before the Trial Court in relation to the said recovery. One of the affidavits
did not bear a date or signature, whereas the other affidavit contained both a date
and a signature. During cross-examination, PW6 stated that the PR No. assigned to
the knife was 195/12, whereas the affidavit dated 11.07.2012 referred to the PR No.
185/12. Further, the affidavit, which bore neither a date nor a signature, stated that
the knife had been recovered near the bank of the canal.
“ප්‍ර: ඒ අනුව මහත්මය ඔබ විසින් භාරයට ගත පිහිය ක ායි ආ ාරකේ පිහියක්ෂද?
උ: මිකටහි තලකයහි මුල් ක ාටක ේ කල් දක්ෂනට ලැබුන. අග උල් වූ පිහියක්ෂ. මිට
ගුරුපාටට හුරු මිට අගල් 4 ක්ෂ පමණ දිගට තලය උල්ව තිබු අතර අගල් 7ක්ෂ පමණ දිග
සිල්වා පාට පිහියක්ෂ.
ප්‍ර: දැන් මහත්මය ඔබ විසින් ඉන්පසුව භාරයට ගත් පිහිය ම්බන්ධකයන් ඔබ ගත්
පියවර කුමක්ෂද?
උ: නඩු බඩු කුවිතන්සිපත් අං 195/12 ට ඇතුලත් ර උපක ේව කපා. ක ා. 30154
රාජපක්ෂෂට භාර දුන්න.” (at vide page 155 of the Appeal Brief)
21. Thus, the evidence of PW6 gives rise to discrepancies concerning, inter alia, the PR
No. assigned to the knife and the precise place from which the knife was allegedly
recovered.
22. Further, it is significant to note that the knife allegedly recovered pursuant to the
statement of the Appellant was never subjected to DNA analysis to determine
whether the identity of the person whose blood was allegedly detected on the knife
belonged to the deceased or otherwise connecting the said knife with the alleged
offence. Notably, there is no scientific evidence establishing that the blood allegedly
found on the knife was, in fact, human blood. Accordingly, the evidentiary value of
the recovered knife in connecting the Appellant with the commission of the alleged
offence is substantially diminished.
8 | P a g e
23. The next witness called by the prosecution was PW2, the younger daughter of the
deceased. At the time of the alleged incident, PW2 was not residing with the
deceased, as she had married and was residing with her husband. However, prior to
her marriage, she had lived with the deceased in the same house for approximately
eight years. According to her evidence, there was a window in the living room of
the house which was not fitted with any grill.
“ප්‍ර: ග්‍රිල් එකහම දල තිබුනද?
උ: ාකල් තිබුන තැන ගහල තිබුකන් නැහැ. ාමර වල ග්‍රිල් තිබ්බා. අම්මකේ ාමකර්
ග්‍රිල් තිබ්බද කියල මත යක්ෂ නැහැ. ඒ වකේ තමා.” (at vide page 113 of the Appeal
Brief)
24. PW10, the Judicial Medical Officer who conducted the post-mortem examination
of the deceased, was also called as a witness for the prosecution. According to his
testimony, he proceeded to the scene of the alleged offence and observed the body
of the deceased at approximately 11.30 a.m. on the next day. Based on the condition
and nature of the body, he opined that the death could have occurred at least 12
hours, or approximately 12-24 hours, prior to the time at which he examined the
body.
25. PW10 identified a total of 15 injuries on the body of the deceased. According to his
evidence, the first injury was a cut injury to the neck, which had severed the thyroid
gland and the trachea. He further opined that, as a consequence of this injury, the
deceased would have been incapable of making any sound. Further, PW10
expressed that the knife produced in evidence was capable of causing all the injuries
observed on the body of the deceased.
26. Since this case is entirely based on circumstantial evidence, it is of paramount
importance to discuss the established legal principles relating to circumstantial
evidence.
9 | P a g e
27. Sir Alfred Wills, in his admirable book “Wills' Circumstantial Evidence” (Chapter
VI), lays down the following rules specially to be observed in the case of
circumstantial evidence:
“1) the facts alleged as the basis of any legal inference must be clearly proved
and beyond reasonable doubt connected with the factum probandum;
2) the burden of proof is always on the party who asserts the existence of any
fact, which infers legal accountability;
3) in all cases, whether of direct or circumstantial evidence the best evidence
must be adduced which the nature of the case admits;
4) in order to justify the inference of guilt, the inculpatory facts must be
incompatible with the innocence of the appellant and incapable of explanation,
upon any other reasonable hypothesis than that of his guilt; and
5) if there be any reasonable doubt of the guilt of the appellant, he is entitled as
of right to be acquitted.”
28. In the case of The Queen v Kularatne 71 NLR at page 534, the Court of Criminal
Appeal quoted with approval the dictum of Whitemeyer, J. In Rex v Blom stated as
follows:
“Two cardinal rules of logic which governs the use of circumstantial evidence in
the criminal trial. (1) The inference sought to be drawn must be consistent with all
the approved facts. If it does not, then the inference cannot be drawn. (2) The proof
of facts should be such that they exclude every reasonable inference from them, save
the one to be drawn. If they had not excluded the other reasonable inferences, then
there must be a doubt whether the inference sought to be drawn is correct.”
29. In Don Sunny v Attorney General [1988] 2Sri LR 1, it was held:
i. When a charge is sought to be proved by circumstantial evidence the proved
items of circumstantial evidence when taken together must irresistibly point
10 | P a g e
towards the only inference that the appellant committed the offence. On a
consideration of all the evidence the only inference that can be arrived at
should be consistent with the guilt of the appellant only.
ii. If on a consideration of the items of circumstantial evidence if an inference
can be drawn which is consistent with the innocence of the appellant, then
one cannot say that the charges have been proved beyond reasonable doubt.
iii. If upon a consideration of the proved items of circumstantial evidence if the
only evidence that can be drawn is that the appellant committed the offence
then they can be found guilty.
iv. The prosecution must prove that no one else other than the appellant had the
opportunity of committing the offence. The appellant can be found guilty only
if the proved items of circumstantial evidence is consistent with their guilt
and inconsistent with their innocence.
30. In Junaiden Mohamed Haaris, vs. Hon. Attorney General, SC Appeal 118/17 SC
(SC minutes 09/11/2018), the Supreme Court observed that;
“The prosecution relied entirely on circumstantial evidence to establish the
charges, for the reason that there were no eyewitnesses to substantiate any of
the charges against the Accused-Appellant. Thus, it was incumbent on the
prosecution to establish that the ‘circumstances’ the prosecution relied on, are
consistent only with the guilt of the accused-appellant and not with any other
hypothesis.”
31. In other words, all facts or circumstances proved by the prosecution must inevitably
and exclusively point to the guilt of the Appellant, and there should be no
circumstances which may reasonably be considered consistent with the innocence
of the Appellant.
32. Hence, I shall now consider whether the circumstantial evidence adduced by the
prosecution is sufficient to establish the guilt of the Appellant beyond reasonable
doubt.
11 | P a g e
33. It is well established that in a case resting solely on circumstantial evidence, the
prosecution must establish a complete chain of circumstances which solely points
to the guilt of the accused. The circumstances proved should be consistent only with
the hypothesis of the guilt of the Appellant and wholly inconsistent with any
reasonable inference of his innocence. It is only when such a chain of evidence is
established that the guilt of the Appellant can be said to be proved beyond
reasonable doubt.
34. The following authorities provide valuable guidance in evaluating the sufficiency
of the circumstantial evidence.
35. In the case of King v Abeywickrema, 44 NLR 254, Soertsz J. remarked thus:
“In order to base a conviction on circumstantial evidence the jury must be
satisfied that the evidence was consistent with the guilt of the accused and
inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of his innocence.”
36. In King v Appuhamy 46 NLR 128, Keuneman J. held thus:
“In order to justify the inference of guilt from purely circumstantial evidence,
the inculpatory facts must be incompatible with the innocence of the accused
and incapable of explanation upon any other reasonable hypothesis than that of
his guilt.”
37. In Gunawardena v. The Republic of Sri Lanka [1981] 2 Sri. LR 315, it was
observed that:
“In a case of circumstantial evidence, the facts given in evidence may, taken
cumulatively be sufficient to rebut the presumption of innocence, although each
fact, when taken separately may be a circumstance of suspicion. Each piece of
circumstantial evidence is not a link in a chain for if one link breaks the chain
would fail. Circumstantial evidence is more like a rope composed of several
12 | P a g e
cords. One strand of rope may be insufficient to sustain the weight but three
stranded together may be quite sufficient.
In a case resting on circumstantial evidence the judge in addition to giving the
usual direction that the prosecution must prove the case beyond reasonable
doubt must give a further direction in express terms that they must not convict
on circumstantial evidence unless they are satisfied that the facts proved are (a)
consistent with the guilt of the accused; and (b) exclude every possible
explanation other than the guilt of the accused.”
38. As observed by Sisira De Abrew J. in Samantha v Republic of Sri Lanka [2010] 2
Sri LR 236;
i. In a case of circumstantial evidence if an inference of guilt is to be drawn
against the accused such inference must be the one and only irresistible and
inescapable inference that the accused committed the crime.
ii. It is the duty of the trial Judge to tell the jury that such evidence must be
totally inconsistent with the innocence of the accused and must only be
consistent with his guilt.
39. In the present case, it is evident that the window in the living room was left open,
was not fitted with a grill, and was capable of being used by a person to enter the
house, as established through the evidence of PW1 and PW2. Further, the main door
of the house was found open on the following morning. The prosecution therefore
failed to establish, by positive evidence, that access to the house was confined to the
Appellant or that no other person could have entered the premises during the
relevant period.
40. Furthermore, the evidence of PW4 cannot be regarded as a reliable circumstance
connecting the Appellant with the commission of the offence. Although PW4
testified that he observed a person similar to the Appellant on the night of the
incident near the residence of the deceased, he did not positively identify that person
13 | P a g e
as the Appellant. On the contrary, during cross-examination, PW4 admitted that he
merely assumed that the person was the Appellant on account of his beard. Thus,
his evidence amounts to no more than an uncertain identification and cannot safely
be relied upon as a positive identification of the Appellant.
41. Therefore, the question arises as to whether the evidence presented by the
prosecution is sufficient to draw the sole inference of the Appellant’s guilt and
whether it is inconsistent with any other inference that could suggest his innocence.
42. When these matters are considered cumulatively, the prosecution evidence leaves
open a reasonable possibility that a person other than the Appellant could have
gained access to the house and committed the offence. In the circumstances, the
evidence adduced by the prosecution falls short of establishing that the Appellant’s
guilt is the one and only irresistible inference that can be drawn from the proved
facts. The reasonable possibility of third-party involvement, coupled with the
unreliable nature of PW4’s identification, therefore breaks the chain of
circumstantial evidence relied upon by the prosecution.
43. Furthermore, it should be noted that the learned High Court Judge expressly stated
that he did not place significant reliance on the recoveries made under Section 27 of
the Evidence Ordinance, as testified to by PW6. Nevertheless, the learned High
Court Judge proceeded to conclude that there was no evidence before the court to
establish that any person other than the Appellant was responsible for the death of
the deceased.
44. The items recovered under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance, based on the
statement made by the Appellant, cannot be treated as conclusive evidence. They
only demonstrate that the Appellant knew the whereabouts of those items.
45. In H. M. Heen Banda v The Queen 75 NLR 54, the Court held that:
“Where part of a statement of an accused person is put in evidence under section
27 of the Evidence Ordinance, it is the duty of the trial Judge to explain to the
14 | P a g e
Jury that such a statement is only evidence of the fact that the accused knew
where the article discovered could be found, and nothing more.”
46. Similarly, in Ranasinghe v Attorney-General [2007] Sri LR 218, it was held inter
alia that:
“…..since discovery is consequence of a section 27 statement only leads to the
conclusion that the accused had the knowledge as to the weapon being kept at
the place from which it was detected;.”
47. When the evidence is considered in its entirety, it does not, in my view, lead to an
irresistible inference of the Appellant’s guilt. This is particularly so in view of the
evidence of PW1 and PW2 regarding the possibility of access to the house by a third
party. Significantly, the prosecution also failed to establish the time of death with
any reasonable degree of precision; the medical evidence only indicates a broad
period within which the death could have occurred, thereby leaving a substantial
interval between the last occasion on which the Appellant was allegedly seen with
the deceased and the discovery of her body.
48. Furthermore, certain notable shortcomings are apparent in the conduct of the
investigation. No attempt was made to trace fingerprints at the scene. More
significantly, although a knife allegedly recovered pursuant to the statement of the
Appellant was never subjected to DNA analysis to determine whether the blood
allegedly found upon it belonged to the deceased or any other person. Thus, there is
no scientific evidence connecting the alleged blood on the knife to the deceased or
otherwise linking the knife to the commission of the offence.
49. The above facts, which render the prosecution’s version doubtful, have escaped the
attention of the learned High Court Judge. More importantly, the absence of such
evidence regarding the precise time of the death precludes the Court from excluding
the possible involvement of persons other than the Appellant. Consequently, the
only inference that can reasonably be drawn from the evidence adduced by the
15 | P a g e
prosecution is not the guilt of the Appellant; rather, it is equally consistent with other
inferences pointing to the innocence of the Appellant. Thus, the case is undoubtedly
a case of some suspicion, and it is not safe to allow the conviction to stand.
50. Additionally, in this matter, the prosecution placed considerable reliance on the last
seen theory, contending that the deceased was last seen in the company of the
Appellant prior to the recovery of her body, and that these circumstances constitute
an incriminating piece of evidence against him.
51. In Sahadevan alias Sagadevan v State represented by Inspector of Police, Chennai
(2003) Vol. 1 SCC 534, the prosecution established the fact that the deceased was
seen in the company of the appellants from the morning of March 5, 1985 till at
least 5 p.m. On that day, he was brought to his house, and thereafter his dead body
was found in the morning of March 6, 1985. In the background of such facts, the
Court observed:
“Therefore, it has become obligatory on the appellants to satisfy the court as to
how, where and in what manner Vadivelu parted company with them. This is on
the principle that a person who is last found in the company of another, if later
found missing, then the person with whom he was last found has to explain the
circumstances in which they parted company. In the instant case the appellants
have failed to discharge this onus. In their statement under Section 313 CrPC,
they have not taken any specific stand whatsoever.”
52. The last seen theory comes into play where the time-gap between the point of time
when the Appellant and the deceased were seen last alive and when the deceased is
found dead is so small that the possibility of any person other than the Appellant
being the author of the crime becomes impossible. It would be difficult in some
cases to positively establish that the deceased was last seen with the Appellant when
there is a long gap and the possibility of other persons coming in between exists. In
the absence of any other positive evidence to conclude that the Appellant and the
16 | P a g e
deceased were last seen together, it would be hazardous to come to a conclusion of
guilt in those cases.
53. In the present case, the Appellant was seen with the deceased at around 7.00 p.m.
on the day of the incident. The body of the deceased was recovered at approximately
7.00 a.m. on the next morning, lying on the bed inside her room, as testified by
PW1. Significantly, the evidence of the JMO provides that the death could have
occurred at least 12 hours, or approximately 12-24 hours, prior to the time at which
he examined the body.
54. According to PW1, there was a window in the living room of the house which was
ordinarily left open and through which a person could enter the premises without
encountering any obstruction. This evidence is further corroborated by PW2, who
testified that the said window was not fitted with any grill. Significantly, on the
following morning, the main door of the house was found to be open. Further,
although PW1 testified that she had closed the doors and windows before going to
bed, she did not specifically testify that she had locked all the doors and windows
of the house so as to prevent access to the premises by any other person.
Accordingly, the evidence regarding the accessibility of the premises does not
exclude the reasonable possibility of a third party gaining entry to the house.
55. What is discernible from the above evidence is that the house could be accessed
through the window in the living room, which was left open and was not fitted with
a grill, and the time of death was not established with certainty by the medical
evidence. In these circumstances, the possibility of another person gaining access to
the house and the deceased cannot be excluded.
56. In Mavelage Sanjeewa Rajapaksha Vs. Attorney General, CA/HCC/0021/2023,
delivered on 03.10.2025, by R.P. Hettiarachchi, J., it was held that;
“In the present case, the Appellant was seen with the deceased at around 9.00
a.m. on the day of the incident. The body of the deceased was recovered at
17 | P a g e
approximately 5.00 p.m. on the same day, lying under a bed inside the house, as
testified by PW3. Significantly, neither the post-mortem report nor the evidence
of the JMO provides any indication of the approximate time of death, and the
prosecution did not seek to question the JMO on this crucial aspect. This
evidentiary gap prevents any definitive conclusion regarding the time of death.”
“Nonetheless, in the present case, the involvement of a third party is clearly
evident, as previously noted. In light of the above evidence, this Court finds it
impossible to apply the “last seen” theory, as there existed a considerable time
gap between the point at which the deceased was last seen in the company of the
Appellant and the subsequent discovery of the body. Additionally, the
involvement of a third party cannot be completely ruled out, as there is evidence
that the deceased’s stepfather had come in between.”
57. The Indian Supreme Court in Digamber Vaishnav & Another v State of
Chhattisgarh (2019) INSC 308 ruled that;
“There must be a reasonable proximity between the time of last seen and the
discovery of the dead body. If the time gap is too large, it introduces doubt about
the appellant’s involvement.”
58. In State of UP v. Satish (2005) (3) SCC 114, the Supreme Court held that;
“The Last Seen Theory applies when the time gap between the appellant’s last
sighting with the victim and the discovery of the victim’s dead body is so small
that no third party could have intervened. If the appellant does not provide a
satisfactory explanation, an adverse inference can be drawn.”
59. The Indian Supreme Court in the case of Surajdeo Mahto vs. The State of Bihar
(Cr A 1677 of 2011 decided on 4th August 2021 – Indian SC) observed that:
“Briefly put, the last seen theory is applied where the time interval between the
point of when the accused and the deceased were last seen together, and when
18 | P a g e
the victim is found dead, is so small that the possibility of any other person other
than the accused being the perpetrator of the crime becomes impossible.”
60. The sum total of the above dicta is that when a case is based on circumstantial
evidence and the prosecution is relying on the last seen theory, the proof of the exact
time of death is of paramount importance. There should be circumstances which
establish that the probable time of death is so small and insignificant that it should
be at or about the time last seen with the accused. The time period the deceased is
found dead should be so small that the possibility of any person other than the
accused being the author of the crime is impossible and that, when all circumstances
are taken into account, it should be highly improbable that anyone other than the
accused could be the perpetrator of the alleged death.
61. Nonetheless, in the present case, the possibility of the involvement of a third party
cannot be completely excluded, as previously noted. In light of the above evidence,
this Court finds it impossible to apply the last seen theory, as there existed a
considerable time gap between the point at which the deceased was last seen in the
company of the Appellant and the subsequent discovery of the body. Additionally,
the involvement of a third party cannot be completely ruled out, as there is evidence
that the window in the living room was left open and the main door was found open
the following morning.
62. In these circumstances, there is a substantial time interval between the last occasion
on which the Appellant was allegedly seen with the deceased and the discovery of
the deceased’s body. Significantly, the evidence shows that a window of the house
was left open and was not fitted with a grill, thereby providing a possible means of
access to the premises by another person during the relevant period. Accordingly,
the possibility of another person gaining access to the house and being involved in
the commission of the offence cannot be excluded. The evidence therefore does not
establish that the Appellant was the person who was necessarily with the deceased
at or immediately before the time of her death.
19 | P a g e
63. Accordingly, the circumstances relied upon by the prosecution do not provide a
sufficiently proximate last seen circumstance from which the guilt of the Appellant
can safely be inferred in the absence of other cogent and independent evidence
connecting him with the commission of the offence. The mere fact that the
Appellant was last seen with the deceased at around 7.00 p.m. cannot, in the
circumstances of the present case, by itself establish that he was the perpetrator of
the crime.
64. For the reasons stated above, I am of the opinion that the Appellant should not have
been convicted of the offence of murder. In the circumstances, the appeal of the
Appellant is allowed, and he is acquitted.
